Hi Kimberly,

Thank you for the materials so far. The RFP review board has a tight checklist and has asked us to provide detailed evidence on the following for Redwood's hosted inference offering:

- Per-endpoint latency quantiles (P50/P90/P95/P99/P99.9) for single-turn text generation at 512 token context, at 1k, 5k, and 10k QPS/harnessed concurrency.
- The exact test harness (versioned scripts, workload generator, seed prompts) used to produce those numbers.
- How caching (prefix + KV) affects tail behavior and a short description of warmup procedures.
- Behavior under graceful degradation: concurrent saturation, fallback to lower-capacity model variants, and the resulting latency distribution.

Can you supply the raw CSVs and the methodology narrative (we prefer artifacts we can replay in-house) by next Friday? Procurement also wants a short summary we can include in the SOW.

From: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek_kulkarni@redwood.ai>
To: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 20 May 2028 12:34:00 -0700
Subject: Re: FW: EdgeFin RFP – request for latency quantiles, test harness, and scaling notes

Kimberly, Karthik —

Attached are the artifacts requested. Summary and methodology below. Files attached: redwood_perf_harness_instructions.pdf, qps_latency_matrix.csv, kv_warmup_profile.json. (Attachment stubs sent from internal lab bucket.)

Summary (for SOW):
Redwood measured single-turn text-generation latency using a reproducible harness (Docker image: redwood/harness:20280520-v1) across two representative model configurations: an optimized 16B quantized variant and a 70B float/quant mix variant. Each run used the same seed prompt corpus (included in the harness) at 512 token context length. Workloads were generated with vegeta-based driver configured for closed-loop concurrency and an open-loop QPS driver for spike tests.

Key methodology points:
- Warmup: for each run we initialize prefix cache and run a 10-minute ramp (50% → target) before measurement. kv_warmup_profile.json contains measured cache-hit fraction over time and guidance for deterministic warm starts.
- Concurrency model: the harness supports both closed-loop (sustained concurrency) and open-loop (burst QPS) modes. Our CSV contains separate rows for closed-loop steady-state at "concurrency targets" (1k, 5k) and an open-loop spike that reached 10k RPS for 3 minutes.
- Metrics captured: per-request wall-clock latency, server-side token-step latency distribution, model decode time, CPU/GPU utilization samples (1s resolution), and batch sizes observed.

Representative results (excerpt from qps_latency_matrix.csv):
- 16B optimized (closed-loop sustained 1k): P50 18 ms, P90 32 ms, P95 40 ms, P99 78 ms, P99.9 210 ms
- 16B optimized (closed-loop sustained 5k): P50 20 ms, P90 45 ms, P95 58 ms, P99 120 ms, P99.9 420 ms
- 16B optimized (open-loop 10k spike): P50 25 ms, P90 92 ms, P95 160 ms, P99 470 ms, P99.9 1,200 ms

- 70B variant (closed-loop sustained 1k): P50 48 ms, P90 110 ms, P95 156 ms, P99 360 ms, P99.9 980 ms

Caching and tail behavior notes:
- Prefix cache reduces token emission latencies by up to 30% at median and materially improves P99 under steady-state when warm (cache-hit fraction > 85%). The kv_warmup_profile shows a ~7–12 minute warm window to reach >80% hit rates depending on request mix.
- Under sudden open-loop spikes without warm cache, P99 and P99.9 inflate significantly due to cold KV lookups and queuing; this is visible in the 10k spike row.

Graceful degradation behavior:
- Primary response: automatic admission control reduces batch sizes and enforces client-level QPS throttles once latency budget is breached. This keeps P99 from becoming unbounded but increases median latency modestly.
- Model-fallback: when admission control is insufficient, policy routes new requests to a smaller model family (16B from 70B) which reduces P99 by approx. 40–60% relative to saturated 70B runs, at the cost of generation quality.
- Region-fallback: if capacity is exhausted in a region, requests are routed to a secondary region with higher network RTT; typical effect: +10–30ms median, P99 increases by a factor of ~1.2–1.5 versus local fallback.

Attached artifacts include the full per-request rows so EdgeFin can compute any additional quantiles. The harness instructions include exact Docker run commands, environment variable mapping, and a masked auth flow you can replace with your own tokens for replay.

If you want, we can also run the same harness against your curated prompt set in our lab (redwood-managed run) and provide the signed CSVs.

Regards,
Vivek Kulkarni
Senior Performance Engineer, Redwood Inference
vivek_kulkarni@redwood.ai

SOW blurb (editable):
Redwood Inference will provide reproducible performance evidence for hosted endpoints, including per-request latency traces and aggregated quantiles at configured concurrency levels. Artifacts include a Docker-based harness (redwood/harness:20280520-v1), the seed prompt corpus used for runs, and raw CSV outputs with per-request timings. Warmup guidance and prefix/KV-cache profiles are included to enable deterministic replays. During capacity saturation, Redwood enforces admission control and supports configurable model-fallback policies (automatic routing to smaller model variants) and cross-region fallbacks; the artifacts show quantile shifts for both degradation modes.

Next steps:
- Let us know whether EdgeFin wants the runs re-executed against your private prompt corpus (we can schedule a managed run).
- Confirm which model family you want evidenced in the final RFP materials (16B, 70B, or both).
